Your mystra_llm_core.js file expects a variable named: apiKey (or something similar) inside its functions.

Node.js does not automatically read the .env file. You need a package, almost certainly dotenv, to do that. The dotenv.config() function must be called before you try to access any process.env variables.

Ensure import dotenv from 'dotenv'; and dotenv.config(); are the very first lines of executable code.

Best Practice: Local vs. Central .env Files
This is a great architecture question. Should you have one master .env file or separate ones for each service?

For security and modern development, your new setup is the better practice.

One Central .env File (The Old Way):

Pro: All secrets are in one place.

Con: It violates a key security principle called the Principle of Least Privilege. Your front-end, your back-end, and any other services would all have access to a single file containing everyone's secrets, even ones they don't need. It's also brittle, as you discovered when you moved the folder.

Separate .env per Service (The Better, Modern Way):

✅ Security: The scroll-server only knows about the secrets it needs to function. If another part of your project were ever compromised, the secrets for this service would remain safe.

✅ Portability: Your scroll-server is now a self-contained module. You can copy its folder anywhere, run npm install, and it will work because its configuration is with it. This is essential for things like Docker and deploying to the cloud.

✅ Simplicity: The code is cleaner. No more complex path.resolve logic.

Recommendation: Stick with your new structure. Having a separate .env file for each independent service (like scroll-server) is the professional standard for building secure and scalable applications. Just make sure that each .env file location is listed in your master .gitignore file.

Your assumption is correct—a local .gitignore will handle it. However, the best practice is even simpler and more robust.

Here’s the breakdown:

How .gitignore Works
Git processes .gitignore files at every directory level, from the root of the repository downwards. Rules in a parent directory's .gitignore apply to all subdirectories.

This means you have two main options:

Local .gitignore: You could put a .gitignore file inside Swerver/backend/scroll-server/ with the line .env. This works perfectly for that specific folder. But, if you create another service elsewhere, you have to remember to create another .gitignore file there.

Master .gitignore: You could put one .gitignore file in your top-level mWorksWebsite/ folder.

The Best Practice (And Simplest Solution)
The most effective and professional approach is to use a master .gitignore at the project root to ignore patterns that apply globally. For .env files, this is the ideal solution.

Do this:

In your absolute top-level project folder (mWorksWebsite/), create a single file named .gitignore if it doesn't already exist.

Add this single line to that file:

Code snippet

# Ignore all .env files in any directory
.env
That's it.

Why this is the best way:

It's Global: This one rule tells Git to ignore any file named .env it finds in the root directory or any subdirectory, no matter how deep.

Set It and Forget It: You never have to think about this again. You can create new services anywhere in your project, add .env files to them, and they will all be automatically and correctly ignored by Git.

It's Cleaner: Your root .gitignore becomes the single source of truth for what should be excluded from your entire project, like node_modules, build output, and secrets.

So, to answer your question directly: While a local file works, the superior method is a single .env entry in your top-level .gitignore. It's less work and impossible to forget.

You are correct, the 404 error is likely because Express isn't yet configured to serve the files the browser is requesting. But you've stumbled upon a more interesting and very common web development puzzle.

Yes, the "sentient font" is being blocked, and you're right to be surprised that it's a local source! Here’s why that happens.

Why a Local Font is Blocked: The Content Security Policy (CSP)
Think of the CSP as a bouncer for your website. It's a security feature that tells the browser, "Only load scripts, styles, and fonts from these approved addresses."

The key issue here is that for security reasons, browsers treat different ports on localhost as different origins.

Your front-end (the HTML page) is likely running on one port (e.g., Vite's default localhost:5173).

Your back-end server (scroll-server) is running on localhost:8080.

The CSP bouncer on your front-end page sees the request for the font coming from a "foreign" address (:8080) and blocks it because it's not on the approved guest list.

How to Fix It
You need to add your server's address (http://localhost:8080) to the font-src guest list in your front-end's CSP.

No, "Sentient" is far from the only one. There are now thousands of variable fonts. Major foundries and platforms like Google Fonts have embraced them.

The technology was officially announced in 2016 as an update to the OpenType specification (version 1.8). However, the core idea is older, building on Adobe's "Multiple Master" font technology from the 1990s.

The Parameters (Axes of Variation)
The "parameters" you can control are called axes. There are five standard, registered axes:

Weight (wght): How thin or bold the font is.

Width (wdth): How narrow or wide the characters are.

Slant (slnt): The angle of obliqueness, usually from 0 to -15 degrees.

Italic (ital): A binary switch (0 for off, 1 for on) that can swap in different character shapes better suited for italics.

Optical Size (opsz): Automatically adjusts the font's weight and spacing for better readability at different sizes (e.g., thicker strokes for tiny text).

Designers can also create any custom axes they can imagine, from changing the height of ascenders (ASCN) to making the font more expressive or "wonky" (WONK).

File Size and Data Storage
Here's a key benefit: a variable font file is often significantly smaller than loading multiple static fonts. For example, loading Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic font files might total 400KB. A single variable font that can produce all those styles and everything in between might only be 150KB.

A font file stores the outline of each character as a set of mathematical vector points (Bézier curves). A variable font stores the default shape of a character and then a series of "deltas" for each axis. A delta is simply an instruction like, "to create the 'Bold' version, move this specific point by this X/Y distance." The browser then interpolates between these deltas to create all the in-between styles. A single font can contain tens of thousands of these data points.

The Theoretical Structure
You asked what structure they graph to. The official term is a design space or variation space.

Think of it as an n-dimensional space where each axis is a dimension.

A font with just a Weight axis is a 1D line.

A font with Weight and Width axes graphs to a 2D plane.

A font with Weight, Width, and Slant graphs to a 3D cube.

Every possible point inside that shape represents a unique, valid style of the font. Your "stack call" from the AI is essentially just feeding coordinates into this design space.

Static vs. Dynamic Routing: The "Dumb Waiter"
The main reason to use express.static is for performance and simplicity.

The reason the back-end server doesn't handle translating the code is because they are two fundamentally different jobs that happen at different times: building the code and running the server.

The Kitchen and the Waiter: Build-Time vs. Run-Time
Think of it like a restaurant.

The Kitchen (Your Build Step): This is where you take raw ingredients (your .tsx source code) and prepare, cook, and plate them into a finished dish (the compiled .js file). This compilation process is complex and takes time. It happens once, before any customers arrive.

The Server (Your Back-End): This is the waiter. The waiter's job is to take the finished dish from the kitchen and deliver it to the customer's table as quickly as possible. The waiter doesn't do any cooking; they just serve what's already been prepared.

Instead, you run the compiler once (the build step) to create the final .js files. Then, your Express back-end (the waiter) can serve those pre-built, optimized files thousands of times per second without breaking a sweat.

Now, let's debug the "first rat in the basement"—the OBS connection. You're right to be suspicious. A "could not connect" error when the server seems to be running is classic jank. It's almost always one of two things: the RTMP service isn't actually listening, or a firewall is blocking the connection.

Let's start our "Level 1" adventure and investigate.

Debugging the RTMP Connection
Step 1: Is the Port Actually Open?
The Swerver.js log shows the HTTP server started, but it doesn't explicitly confirm the RTMP server did. Let's verify if anything is listening on port 1935.

Leave your Swerver.js running.

Open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window.

Run this command and press Enter:

Bash

netstat -ano | findstr ":1935"
Analyze the Output:

If you see a line that contains LISTENING, then the server is working correctly, and the problem is likely the firewall or OBS settings.

If the command returns nothing, it means the RTMP portion of our Swerver.js failed to start.

Step 2: Is the Firewall Blocking the Port? (Most Likely Culprit)
This is the most common cause for this exact problem. Your code is trying to open a port, and Windows Firewall is blocking it without telling you.

Click the Start Menu and type "Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security" and open it.

In the new window, click on "Inbound Rules" on the left.

Look through the list for any rules named "Node.js" or "Node.js JavaScript Runtime".

Check the "Action" column. If any of them say Block, that's our problem. You'll need to right-click the rule, go to properties, and change the action to "Allow the connection".

If a rule doesn't exist, the firewall should pop up a permission dialog the first time you run Swerver.js. It's possible it was accidentally denied.

Step 3: Double-Check OBS Settings
Just to be certain, confirm your settings in OBS (Settings -> Stream):

Service: Custom...

Server: rtmp://localhost:1935/live
